kid.question: What does Lamentations 3:26 commend while seeking God's salvation?

options.text: Hoping and waiting quietly for Him
Singing and bringing gifts before Him
Assembling and offering prayers together
Fasting and confessing sins before Him

kid.explanation: The poem commends seeking the Lord and quietly hoping and waiting for His salvation.

kid.question: When does the poem say it is good to bear a yoke?

options.text: After winning a battle
At the year's harvest
During one's youth
Before a royal feast

kid.explanation: The speaker says it is good for a person to bear the yoke in youth.

kid.question: What hope is given to someone who feels rejected?

options.text: The Lord will send a new king immediately
The Lord will explain the sorrow that night
The Lord will prevent another person's tears
The Lord will show compassion again

kid.explanation: The Lord will not cast off forever; even though He causes grief, He will have compassion according to His mercies.

kid.question: Which treatment does Lamentations 3:34-36 condemn?

options.text: Stealing grain from a neighbor
Denying someone a fair hearing
Refusing shelter to a traveler
Breaking a promise to a friend

kid.explanation: The poem rejects crushing prisoners, turning aside a person's right, and subverting a person's cause.

kid.question: What should the people do after examining their ways?

options.text: Turn again to the Lord
Wait for others to change
Blame the neighboring nations
Appoint a different royal family

kid.explanation: The people are urged to search and test their ways and turn again to the Lord.

kid.question: What should people lift to God along with their hands?

options.text: Their crowns
Their swords
Their harvests
Their hearts

kid.explanation: The appeal says to lift up the heart with the hands to God in heaven.

kid.question: What makes the speaker's eyes run like rivers in Lamentations 3:48?

options.text: The loss of his father's farm
The destruction of his own people
The betrayal by his own brothers
The death of a foreign king

kid.explanation: His eyes run with rivers of water for the destruction of his people, and he continues until the Lord looks down.

kid.question: What animal pictures the speaker being chased?

options.text: A deer chased by lions
A sheep chased by wolves
A bird chased by hunters
A fish chased through nets

kid.explanation: The speaker says his enemies chased him like a bird without cause.

kid.question: From where does the speaker call God's name?

options.text: From a city watchtower
From a crowded temple
From a distant battlefield
From a deep dungeon

kid.explanation: He calls to the Lord from the low dungeon.

kid.question: What does the Lord say when He draws near?

options.text: Return to your home
Do not be afraid
Wait beside the gate
Speak before the king

kid.explanation: The speaker recalls that the Lord drew near when he called and said not to fear.

high-school.question: How is waiting portrayed in the counsel about bearing hardship?

options.text: Hopeful seeking is postponed until every public insult has been avenged
Quietness is recommended as proof that God no longer hears prayer
Hopeful seeking is joined to quietness and humble endurance
Quietness is demanded so that the rulers cannot learn about the suffering

high-school.explanation: The passage joins seeking and waiting for salvation with bearing the yoke, silence, dust, and reproach.

high-school.question: What limits the despair that grief might produce?

options.text: Rejection is not final and compassion remains grounded in divine mercy
Grief proves the sufferer has already received every promised blessing
Rejection ends whenever the sufferer can explain the cause of the hardship
Grief means the Lord has transferred His concern to the surrounding nations

high-school.explanation: The Lord will not cast off forever, will have compassion, and does not willingly grieve people.

high-school.question: What standard is affirmed despite the surrounding account of affliction?

options.text: God requires sufferers to surrender their right to be heard
God approves a successful ruler's treatment of captive people
God restricts fair treatment to people with political freedom
God disapproves of crushing prisoners and denying people justice

high-school.explanation: The verses name crushing prisoners, denying rights, and subverting a cause as things the Lord does not approve.

high-school.question: Which response does the communal appeal in Lamentations 3:40-42 call for?

options.text: Fasting, public assembly, and renewed offerings at the temple
Self-examination, return to God, and acknowledgment of rebellion
Pilgrimage, payment of vows, and intercession by the tribal elders
Mourning, burial of the dead, and rebuilding the ruined sanctuary

high-school.explanation: The text turns from complaint about punishment for sins to testing one's ways, returning to God, and confessing transgression.

high-school.question: What tension follows the call to raise hearts and hands?

options.text: The praying people receive immediate news that their city has been rebuilt
The praying people discover that their enemies have confessed on their behalf
The praying people confess rebellion and describe prayer as blocked
The praying people abandon confession after receiving praise from the king

high-school.explanation: The appeal to lift heart and hands is followed by confession, unpardoned guilt, anger, and the image of a cloud blocking prayer.

high-school.question: What does the speaker's sustained weeping express?

options.text: Grief for the people's destruction while awaiting the Lord's notice
Regret at losing office while seeking another public appointment
Anger at failed crops while planning to purchase another field
Disappointment at delayed travel while waiting for foreign messengers

high-school.explanation: The tears concern the destruction of his people and continue until the Lord looks down from heaven.

high-school.question: How does the speaker respond to the experience of being trapped and overwhelmed?

options.text: He accepts the enemies' charge and promises to join their army
He asks the city's rulers to exchange him for royal prisoners
He waits for a sign that his enemies have already departed
He calls on the Lord from the depth of his confinement

high-school.explanation: The account moves from pursuit, a dungeon, and waters over his head to calling on the Lord's name.

high-school.question: How is divine help described after the cry from confinement?

options.text: The Lord sends a ruler, prescribes a payment, and rebuilds the city
The Lord hears, draws near, speaks reassurance, and redeems life
The Lord condemns the cry, withdraws further, and demands public silence
The Lord grants political office, restores wealth, and punishes rival priests

high-school.explanation: The speaker recalls being heard, the Lord's nearness and 'Fear not,' and the pleading and redemption of his life.

high-school.question: Why does the speaker ask God to judge his cause?

options.text: God has seen the wrong and heard the enemies' persistent hostile reproach
God has appointed the enemies to investigate the speaker's complaint
The speaker has already received a favorable verdict from the city court
The speaker's companions have withdrawn every accusation against the enemies

high-school.explanation: The appeal rests on God's seeing the wrong, vengeance, and plots and hearing reproach and hostile speech.

high-school.question: How does the assigned reading end?

options.text: With a report that the enemies have returned everything they took
With a plea for judgment on those who harmed the speaker
With a promise that the ruined city will be rebuilt that day
With an invitation for the enemies to join the evening sacrifice

high-school.explanation: The conclusion asks God to repay according to the enemies' deeds and to pursue and destroy them in anger.

expert.question: What distinguishes the endorsed quietness from a claim that hope has ended?

options.text: Silence and submission replace seeking because salvation is declared unavailable
Silence and submission appear within continued seeking and expectation of salvation
The speaker's quietness is a strategy for concealing an approaching military attack
The speaker's quietness follows a report that every cause of suffering has disappeared

expert.explanation: Waiting, seeking, and hoping frame the counsel to bear a yoke, sit quietly, and endure reproach.

expert.question: How does the passage qualify the Lord's agency in grief?

options.text: Causing grief is denied once the speaker acknowledges that the enemies acted unjustly
Divine compassion is postponed until human beings can prevent every further transgression
Divine compassion is limited to those who have never experienced rejection or reproach
Causing grief is held together with enduring mercy and no willing delight in affliction

expert.explanation: The verses say He may cause grief yet will have compassion, will not cast off forever, and does not afflict willingly.

expert.question: How are divine sovereignty and human injustice distinguished?

options.text: God's command governs events while abuses of prisoners and justice meet His disapproval
God's command governs events so abuses of prisoners necessarily receive His approval
Human courts govern events so divine authority applies only to the speaker's private grief
Human courts govern events while God's concern is confined to the restoration of festivals

expert.explanation: The text disapproves oppression and subverted justice, then asks who can bring things to pass without the Lord's command.

expert.question: How does the speaker move from Lamentations 3:39 into verses 40-42?

options.text: A question about a person's complaint leads to shared accusations against foreign rulers
A quotation from a royal counselor leads to a collective lament for fallen soldiers
A question about a person's complaint leads to shared examination and confession
A command to the temple priests leads to a collective account of ruined festivals

expert.explanation: The singular reflection about punishment for sins is followed by 'let us' examine and return and 'we' have transgressed.

expert.question: Why should the call to return not be read as a report that reconciliation is already complete?

options.text: Confession is followed by a declaration that every prayer has received its requested answer
The command to examine one's ways is addressed only to enemies outside the covenant
Confession is followed by unpardoned guilt and the image of prayer blocked by a cloud
The command to examine one's ways is withdrawn before the people can acknowledge rebellion

expert.explanation: The people confess rebellion and say God has not pardoned, then describe anger and a cloud preventing prayer from passing through.

expert.question: How are the speaker's eyes and the Lord's looking related?

options.text: Human weeping ends because the Lord declares further lament unnecessary
Human weeping persists while awaiting divine attention from heaven
The speaker's tears replace divine attention to the city's suffering
The speaker's tears establish that the city's daughters are already restored

expert.explanation: The eye weeps without interruption until the Lord looks down and beholds from heaven; the sight of the city's suffering affects the heart.

expert.question: What movement takes the speaker from the language of being cut off to renewed life?

options.text: A cry from confinement receives hearing, nearness, reassurance, and redemption
A denial of confinement receives confirmation that the enemies' accusations were correct
A pledge of silence receives a royal appointment and release from civic responsibilities
A report of escape receives instructions to return to the enemies for military service

expert.explanation: After waters rise over his head and he says he is cut off, he calls on the Lord and recalls hearing, nearness, and redeemed life.

expert.question: How does the legal vocabulary deepen the appeal beyond physical rescue?

options.text: The Lord who pleaded for his life delegates the case to the same enemies who pursued him
The speaker treats physical rescue as proof that no further wrong requires divine attention
The speaker withdraws the legal complaint once the enemies acknowledge his former authority
The Lord who pleaded for his life is asked to judge the wrongs and plots against him

expert.explanation: The Lord has pleaded the causes of his soul; the speaker then asks Him to judge his cause, citing seen wrong and heard reproach.

expert.question: How can admitted communal sin coexist with the later claim of causeless pursuit?

options.text: Communal confession proves that the speaker's enemies have received a favorable verdict
The earlier confession is retracted when the speaker starts describing personal suffering
Communal confession does not make every enemy action against the speaker just
The earlier confession applies to a different nation that never appears in the lament

expert.explanation: The passage confesses communal rebellion yet later calls the enemies' pursuit causeless; judgment does not approve each hostile action.

expert.question: What remains unresolved after the recalled reassurance and redemption?

options.text: The speaker still seeks judgment against ongoing reproach and hostile plotting
The speaker has yet to hear whether the Lord received his cry from confinement
The speaker still needs to learn whether the Lord is able to draw near to him
The speaker has yet to decide whether to acknowledge any divine involvement in his life

expert.explanation: Recalled hearing, nearness, and redemption are followed by appeals concerning wrong, plots, reproach, and recompense. The ending remains a plea for judgment.
